name: Vera Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Vera, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner in an underground coal mine. It's a machine with a big spinning drum on the front that cuts the coal straight off the face and loads it onto a shuttle car behind. I'm the lead operator on B crew, so I set the cut sequence with the deputy and keep an eye on the roof bolters. Day starts at six with the gas readings, and then it's cutting, bolting, moving, cutting. I've done it five years and I could do it with my eyes shut, which you shouldn't, obviously.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same. Same crew, same machine, same smell of wet coal. What wears me out is the forty-minute drive in the dark and the paperwork that keeps getting longer. I rent a cottage off my uncle on the edge of town with my dog, Biscuit, and coming home to her is the best part of the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. Sounds like a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go. I'm not one for big opinions online, I mostly post pictures of Biscuit. At work I'd probably just nod when someone brought it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. I don't use any of that AI stuff and I don't want to. If it stays a fancy search box for office people, that suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Same shifts, same savings, I've got about four months of bills put away. Maybe I'd finally replace the pickup's tyres before winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your mine that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coal, mostly. The mine's got a closure plan for the late 2030s anyway, because of the power stations switching over. So my worry was never really robots, it's that coal has an end date. That's been true since I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think about that end date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't, much. It's twelve years away. I figure I'll work it out at thirty-five. My dad says that's how I do everything, leave it until the deputy's standing over me, and he's not wrong.

S0.say: Well, there you go. I'm not one for big opinions online, I mostly post pictures of my dog, and at work I'd just nod along.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I don't use AI and I don't want to. If it stays a fancy search box for office people, that suits me fine.
S0.do: Keeps the same shifts and the same savings, at about four months of bills. Replaces the pickup's tyres before winter and changes nothing else.
S0.quote: My worry was never really robots, it's that coal has an end date.
S0.fieldNote: Vera's main background worry is the planned closure of her coal mine in the late 2030s, not AI. She openly puts off big decisions until she has to make them. Her life is small and steady by choice, built around her crew and her dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be sensible about it. I wouldn't be one of the ones shouting. If the company had a plan, I'd want to see it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry. They already run some continuous miners from a cabin back from the face at other pits. Once it's proven safer, and it would be, the inspectors would almost push them to do it. I'm good at what I do, but I'm good at doing it sitting on the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much at first, I'd wait until the company said something. If they offered the remote training I'd do it, because the alternative's worse, but I wouldn't go looking for it. I'd stop the pickup upgrade I was thinking about and put that money in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like hearing the roof work, that cracking sound. You don't run, but you listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the inspectors would almost push for it. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair, honestly. Nobody I know has been hurt, but my grandad lost two fingers on a belt. If a remote cabin keeps people out from under unsupported roof, I can't argue with that. I just don't want to be the one in the cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then it's a screen and a joystick, and I'd be learning it from some twenty-year-old engineer who's never smelt a coal face. I know that's stubborn. My mum says stubborn is the family business.

S1.say: It's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be sensible about it. If the company had a plan, I'd want to see it in writing.
S1.think: They already run continuous miners from a cabin at other pits, and once it's proven safer, the inspectors will push for it. I'm good at what I do, but I'm good at doing it sitting on the machine.
S1.do: Waits for the company to announce a plan before acting, and would take remote training if offered but wouldn't seek it out. Drops the planned pickup upgrade and puts that money into savings instead.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing the roof work: you don't run, but you listen.
S1.quote: You don't run, but you listen.
S1.fieldNote: Vera's pragmatism means she accepts remote mining as safer and can't argue against it, even while she doesn't want it for herself. Her instinct is to wait for the company to move first. She admits her stubbornness with some humour and a family story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oh, hell. Sorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone needs to slow it down, the government, someone. I'm not political, but that's too fast for anyone. At work I'd say it straight: we're all in the same boat, so let's not turn on each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm done. I don't have anything else. I've got a diploma in mining operations, a pickup and a dog. I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent, food and Biscuit. I'd ask my uncle if I could pay less rent for a while, or move into the spare room at my parents'. I'd go to the union meetings, which I mostly skip, because they'd be the only ones with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a gas alarm at the face. You stop everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not enough to change who I am. I don't learn new things fast, I never have, it took me two years to get good on the miner. So two years is the time it takes me to learn one thing, and there wouldn't be a thing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you mostly skip union meetings. What would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being scared. I'm a middle-of-the-road person, I don't like people yelling. But if the union was the only group asking for redundancy pay or a public income, I'd go and sit at the back. I'd even vote for whoever had an actual plan, whichever side.

S2.say: Someone needs to slow it down, the government or someone, because that's too fast for anyone. We're all in the same boat, so let's not turn on each other.
S2.think: It means I'm done, and I don't have anything else. I've got a diploma in mining operations, a pickup and a dog, and I wouldn't know where to start.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent, food and the dog, and asks her uncle for lower rent or moves into her parents' spare room. Starts going to the union meetings she usually skips, and votes for whichever side has an actual plan.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a gas alarm at the face: you stop everything.
S2.quote: I've got a diploma in mining operations, a pickup and a dog. I wouldn't know where to start.
S2.fieldNote: With two years Vera sees no route out, because she learns slowly and every route would be gone. She turns to family and the union, which she normally avoids. Her centre politics shows in voting for any side with a practical plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five. Okay. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, let's not waste them yelling. Get the government and the companies to agree on something sensible. I'd probably say that once at the tea break and then leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years doesn't help me as much as you'd think. I'm slow to change. I'd probably spend the first two years telling myself it won't really happen to us, and then have three years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save harder, maybe get to eight months. I'd ask the company about training into something hands-on that would last, like mine rescue or the electrical side. But honestly I'd likely wait the first year to see if the robots actually show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Slower, but the same feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell yourself it won't happen. You know that about yourself. Would knowing it change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if someone made me. If my dad sat me down, or the union, and said Vera, sign here. I'm good when there's a form to fill in and a date. I'm bad at making the date myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose that isn't money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew. We've got a group chat for B crew, it's mostly bad jokes and photos of fish. Some of them I see more than my family. If it all goes, I don't know who I'd talk to on a Tuesday.

S3.say: We've got a few years, so let's not waste them yelling. Get the government and companies to agree on something sensible.
S3.think: Five years doesn't help me as much as you'd think, because I'm slow to change. I'd spend two years telling myself it won't happen to us, and then have three years left.
S3.do: Tries to save harder, aiming for eight months of bills, and asks the company about training into mine rescue or electrical work. Likely waits the first year to see whether the robots really arrive.
S3.feel: Alarmed, the same feeling as the faster picture, just slower.
S3.quote: I'm good when there's a form to fill in and a date. I'm bad at making the date myself.
S3.fieldNote: Vera is clear-eyed about her own habit of delay and says extra time might be wasted on denial. She thinks an outside push, family, union or a deadline, would get her moving. Losing her crew, more than her pay, seemed to be the deepest loss for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's about when coal finishes anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a fair amount of time, and the sensible thing is to plan. The mine was closing in the late thirties anyway, so this just lines up. I'd probably say that to the crew to calm people down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is my coal plan, just with a different reason. I always said I'd figure it out at thirty-five. Now I'd have to, and there'd be less to figure out into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep cutting coal and keep saving. I'd probably do my electrical ticket over two or three years, part-time, because the company pays for it. I wouldn't move or change anything big, I'd watch what happens at the other pits first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicky, just a weight that doesn't go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different between the ten-year picture and the two-year one, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I can do one thing properly, which is about my speed. One ticket, slowly, with Biscuit snoring on the couch. In two years I can't do anything, just watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still rent from your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd never leave that cottage if I could help it. Maybe I'd try to buy it off him in a few years, if he'd sell. At least then I'd have somewhere that's mine when the rest goes.

S4.say: That's a fair amount of time, and the sensible thing is to plan. The mine was closing in the late thirties anyway, so this just lines up.
S4.think: Ten years is my coal plan with a different reason. I always said I'd figure it out at thirty-five, and now I'd have to, with less to figure out into.
S4.do: Keeps cutting coal and saving through the first year. Starts a company-paid electrical ticket part-time over two or three years, avoids big changes while watching other pits, and hopes to buy her uncle's cottage in a few years.
S4.feel: Anxious, a steady weight that doesn't go away.
S4.quote: One ticket, slowly, with Biscuit snoring on the couch.
S4.fieldNote: For Vera, ten years matches the coal closure she had already half planned for, so the shock is smaller. She can manage one change at her own pace and picks a single company-paid ticket. Owning her cottage is the security she reaches for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm slow, I know that, and that one doesn't let you be slow. What would help is someone giving me a clear date and a clear form: here's your redundancy, here's the course, here's when it starts. And keeping a crew together somehow, even if it's for different work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the dogs. I'm half joking. But a lot of us out here live alone with a dog and a pickup. If you take the job away, you take away the only reason a lot of people leave the house.

headlineQuote: If you take the job away, you take away the only reason a lot of people leave the house.
portrait: Vera Alvarez is 27 and the lead continuous miner operator on her crew at an underground coal mine. She lives alone with her dog Biscuit in a cottage she rents from her uncle, and has about four months of bills saved. She prefers the familiar, never uses AI, and knows she tends to put off decisions until she must. Her pragmatic politics mean she blames no one in particular and backs whoever has a sensible plan. She sees remote mining as safer but doesn't want it for herself, and the fast AGI scenario leaves her alarmed with nowhere to start, while ten years lines up with a coal closure she was already expecting.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she's slow to change and that scenario doesn't allow it.
whatWouldHelp: A clear date and clear paperwork for redundancy and training, and some way to keep a crew together, even doing different work.
